issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient also directly sustained major physical injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoidance of medical cues can fit some trauma-to-a-loved-one cases, but in this profile it appears to be driven by a personal bodily injury/medical trauma theme that is otherwise unsupported except by the implausible physical-vulnerability appraisal, making this item clinically incoherent with the rest of the profile.

vignette: Sister Maryellen, a 55-year-old nun, has been struggling with profound emotional distress since her brother's tragic death in a car accident two years ago. Sister Maryellen had come to believe that she could have prevented the incident if she had acted differently, and this belief has become a constant source of self-blame and doubt about her ability to protect those she loves. Sister Maryellen's negative appraisals led her to adopt various maladaptive strategies to cope with her distress. She began avoiding places associated with her brother's accident and any reminders of him. Whenever she saw something that reminded her of him, it felt as if a knife had been plunged into her heart, triggering vivid and detailed memories of the event without warning. The clarity of these memories was both haunting and painful; some moments were crystal clear, while others remained shrouded in blankness, leaving her feeling helpless. These memories often surfaced unexpectedly, triggered by seemingly mundane things like the sound of a car door slamming or seeing someone who looked similar to her brother. Each time this happened, Sister Maryellen felt overwhelmed with grief and fear. She began performing mental rituals, such as repeating prayers or silently reciting phrases she believed would prevent another tragedy from occurring. These behaviors served as a desperate attempt to regain control over her life, but they only reinforced her negative beliefs about herself. As the months passed, these maladaptive strategies became deeply ingrained habits that further entrenched her negative appraisals. Avoiding the site of the accident and anything related to her brother led to an increasing sense of isolation. Sister Maryellen's world grew smaller as she distanced herself from places and people who reminded her of her brother, believing that this would somehow protect her from more pain. Her self-blame intensified each time she encountered a trigger or remembered details of the event. The clarity of some memories made it impossible for her to believe that the accident could have been anyone's fault but her own. She felt increasingly unable to rely on herself in moments of crisis, perpetuating a vicious cycle where her negative beliefs fueled her maladaptive behaviors and vice versa. Sister Maryellen's relationships were also affected by these changes. Her husband noticed her withdrawal and growing anxiety but struggled to understand the depth of her pain. He had encouraged her to seek help multiple times, but she was hesitant, fearing that opening up about her grief would only lead to more painful memories. Finally, after a particularly distressing episode triggered by a routine visit to the church where her brother used to volunteer, Sister Maryellen realized that her coping mechanisms were no longer sustainable. The clarity of the memories and the overwhelming sense of self-blame had become too much for her to bear alone. She decided it was time to seek professional help, hoping to find a way to break the cycle of negative appraisals and maladaptive strategies. Sister Maryellen's most pressing fear is that she will continue to blame herself for what happened, believing that her actions led to her brother's death. However, she also harbors a deep hope that through therapy, she can learn to process her grief in a healthier way and regain some sense of control over her life.
